newsitem.title: MEXICO: Late Mexican bid may be anti-privatization hoax.
newsitem.headline: Late Mexican bid may be anti-privatization hoax.

text.p: A late, disqualified entry for the privatization of Mexico's Northeast Railway startled the winning operators, although the bid seems to have been a cry of protest to the country's privatization process.

Representatives from Transportacion Maritima Mexicana (TMM) and Kansas City Southern Industries Inc, the rail line's winning bidders, investigated the mysterious bid and said it appeared to be orchestrated by a phantom organization.

Days after the 50-year operating concession was awarded, a company called Consorcio Desarollo Economico Mexicano (Codemex) sent statements to local media saying it had offered 12.5 billion pesos for the Northeast Railway and the Chihuahua-Pacifico line.
TMM and Kansas City's winning bid was a surprising 11.07 billion pesos ($1.4 billion), almost three times those of the other two bidders.

"Every privatization these guys (Codemex) try to overmatch the winning bid. It's a game. If we took them seriously they would have won Telefonos de Mexico (SA) 80 percent of the banks and all the mining companies," Communication and Transport Ministry (SCT) privatization coordinator Jorge Silberstein told Reuters.

He said the group's origins are unknown and the SCT said it had no information on Codemex or its bid. The ministry said the tardy bid would be rejected because Codemex had not entered months of privatization procedures for the rail.

TMM and Kansas City spokesmen who asked not to be named said a visit to Codemex's offices found a lone representative in a small shared office space. No one answered at the Codemex number listed on its press statement.

Codemex said it is supported by the National Railroad Workers Union, and the bid could be a move to save jobs expected to be cut by the rail's new operators. The union could not be reached for comment. About 40,000 railroad workers have been laid off since 1990 in a move to improve efficiency.
State-owned railroad operator Ferrocarriles Nacionales de Mexico is still considered to be overstaffed with 46,000 workers.
While Mexican law allows workers' organizations to match the best offer in privatizations, Silberstein said workers must formally enter the bidding process.
In a statement, the company said also it was backed by United Pacific Technologies, a subsidiary of Union Pacific Corp.
"Codemex confirms that it has the support of the new company to be created by Union Pacific Technologies in railroad systems programming and development," the statement said.

Union Pacific Technologies has worked on installing a computer highway on Mexico's railways and promised to support any winning concessionaires in the privatisation of the nation's rail track, said Union Pacific spokesman Mark Davis.
However, the Union Pacific subsidiary had never head of the company before receiving calls from press and companies, he said.
Union Pacific had submitted a bid for the Northeast Railway with Mexican construction company ICA.
